title: The Drowning Child
objective: After this level you can apply Peter Singer’s drowning child argument to the question of how much we owe distant strangers, and weigh the main replies.
summary: Singer’s 1972 shallow pond supports a rescue principle he applies to distant suffering; critics press the demandingness objection.

cards.headline: You’d ruin your clothes to save a drowning child. Peter Singer has a follow-up.
cards.body: Almost everyone answers the first question the same way. Singer’s 1972 essay asks what that answer commits you to.

cards.headline: The shallow pond
cards.body: In “Famine, Affluence, and Morality” (1972), Peter Singer pictures walking past a shallow pond and seeing a child drowning. You ought to wade in, he says, even though your clothes get muddy. The mud is insignificant; the child’s death would be very bad. Walking past strikes most people as monstrous. So far, nobody argues.

cards.headline: From pond to principle
cards.body: Singer’s argument runs on premises. If it is in our power to prevent something very bad without sacrificing anything morally significant, we ought to do it. Suffering and death from lack of food, shelter or medical care are very bad. We can prevent some of it by giving. So, he concludes, we are all like the person passing the pond: the cost of a new shirt or a night out can mean the difference between life and death for someone elsewhere.

cards.headline: Far away still counts
cards.body: Singer argued that distance makes no moral difference. A person in need far away counts as much as the child in front of you, because what matters is your ability to help at little cost to yourself. The pond is just the case where you can’t miss it.

cards.headline: Too much to ask?
cards.body: The most common criticism is the demandingness objection. Commonsense morality treats charity as good but optional, critics say, and the world’s needs never stop: a pond you pass once is not a world of endless ponds, and helping every time would take over your life. Singer’s defenders reply that his moderate principle asks you to give up only what isn’t morally significant, which leaves room for the projects that matter most to you.

cards.headline: The Drowning Child: the big picture
learned: His principle: prevent the very bad at small cost
He argued distance makes no moral difference

questions.prompt: In Singer’s 1972 shallow-pond case, what does saving the drowning child cost you?

options.label: Your own safety
options.rationale: The pond is shallow; there is no risk to you.

options.label: A large donation
options.rationale: Money comes later in the argument.

questions.explanation: Saving the child means getting your clothes muddy, which Singer calls insignificant next to the child’s death.

questions.prompt: You’re about to pay for a night out you’d barely remember. What does Singer’s principle imply about that money?

options.label: Give it to prevent something very bad, since it isn’t morally significant
Spend it freely, since the people it could help live far away from you
options.rationale: Singer denies that distance makes a difference.

options.label: Give it only if everyone else in your position gives their share too
options.rationale: Singer’s principle doesn’t depend on others.

options.label: Keep it, since helping strangers is generous but always optional
options.rationale: That is the critics’ view, not Singer’s.

questions.explanation: Singer’s principle says that if you can prevent something very bad without sacrificing anything morally significant, you ought to, and he counts a night out as such a cost.

questions.prompt: Singer lays out premises that lead to a conclusion about giving. What does Level 1 call that structure?

options.label: A controlled experiment
options.rationale: Nothing is tested in a lab.

options.label: A thought experiment
options.rationale: The pond is one, but the premises-to-conclusion structure has another name.

options.label: An opinion poll
options.rationale: Polls show what people think, not whether it follows.

questions.explanation: Level 1 defines an argument as reasons, called premises, laid out to support a conclusion: exactly how Singer’s case is built.
